newsitem.title: GERMANY: East German miners picket Bonn in fight for jobs.
newsitem.headline: East German miners picket Bonn in fight for jobs.

text.p: Thousands of miners from eastern Germany protested outside Bonn's Finance Ministry on Thursday against planned cuts in aid they fear could cost 4,000 jobs in areas already hard-hit by unemployment.
The demonstration came a month after west German miners besieged Bonn's government quarter, finally winning concessions over planned subsidy cuts.
Their victory appeared particularly handsome to those in the east, many of whom lost their jobs after German unification.

The head of IG Bergbau mining union in Brandenburg, the state surrounding Berlin, Ullrich Freese, told a crowd of about 4,000 there was no division between the hard coal industry of western Germany and lignite or soft coal miners of the east.

"We miners in the west and the east will not be played off against each other. We are faced with the same problem across the whole of Germany," Freese told the crowd, which also included a number of west German miners.

Opposition Social Democrat (SPD) leader Oskar Lafontaine and the party's parliamentary chief Rudolf Scharping joined national miners' union leader Hans Berger outside the ministry to address the protesters. The SPD traditionally enjoys the miners' support.
Before unification in 1990 the east German coal industry employed about 130,000 people, but between 1990 and 1995 production dropped by 64 percent and the workforce was decimated.
Now only 18,000 are employed in the industry. A further 13,000 redundant miners work on schemes to restore or redevelop land damaged by decades of open-cast mining.
The government and regional states had pledged 1.5 billion marks ($874 million) a year for maintain these schemes from 1993 to 1997.

But talks to renegotiate a further five years' aid ended inconclusively on Monday after Bonn, under pressure to tighten its budgets to qualify for European monetary union (EMU) in 1999, insisted on reducing its contribution.
Bonn had paid one billion marks and the rest came from the states and east German retraining schemes. The regions want Bonn to hold payments at previous levels.
East German miners say they need even more and demanded two billion marks a year to help create more jobs in areas like Lausitz in Brandenburg, where almost a third of the workforce are out of work.

"The west German miners showed us what to do and we are doing exactly the same to make the government realise how desperate the situation is," said ex-miner Hans-Juergen Haessler, 55, from Seftenberg in the Lausitz region. ($ = 1.716 German Marks)
